specPoints.text: know that current is the rate of flow of charge
know that electric current in solid metallic conductors is a flow of negatively charged electrons
know and use the relationship between charge, current and time: charge = current × time Q = I × t

primer.text: Switch on a lamp and billions of tiny charges begin drifting through the copper — that drift is what we call electric current. This note defines current, counts it in amperes and coulombs, and then links the charge delivered to the current and the time with a compact equation. It also separates the conventional direction engineers use from the electron drift that actually carries the charge.

lessons.title: Current
lessons.opening: Picture a garden hose: the water company does not care how fast one drop goes, only how much water passes the tap each second. Electric current is the same idea for charge. This lesson defines the ampere, follows the conventional direction around the loop, and meets the meter that reads it.
keyPoints: Current is the rate at which electric charge flows through a component.
Current is measured in amperes (A): one ampere is one coulomb of charge per second.
Current flows around a complete circuit from the positive terminal of a cell to the negative one.
An ammeter reads the current and must sit in series with the component being measured.

low.restatement: Current counts how much charge squeezes past a point each second — more charge per second means a bigger current.
low.analogy: Think of counting cars past a roundabout: current is the traffic count per second, not the speed of any single car.
low.examPointer: Quote the unit as amperes (A); if a question says amps, keep the symbol A in your working.

medium.restatement: The definition is a ratio — charge divided by time — so a 2 A reading means 2 coulombs arrive every single second.
medium.analogy: A turnstile tally: the charge is the crowd, the time is how long the gate stays open, and the current is the tally per second.
medium.examPointer: Exams expect conventional current (positive to negative); mention electron drift only when the question asks about charge carriers.

options.text: the energy transferred per unit charge
options.explanation: That is the definition of voltage, not current.

options.text: how fast electric charge streams past a point
options.explanation: Current counts how much charge passes each second.

options.text: the force pushing electrons through a wire
options.explanation: No force appears anywhere in the definition of current.

options.text: the number of electrons sitting inside a wire
options.explanation: Owning electrons is not the same as moving them; current needs flow.

options.text: one joule of energy carried by one coulomb
options.explanation: A joule per coulomb defines a volt.

options.text: one volt across one ohm of resistance
options.explanation: That combination belongs to the voltage-current-resistance equation, not the ampere.

options.text: one watt delivered for one second
options.explanation: A watt times a second is a joule of energy, not a flow of charge.

options.text: one coulomb of charge flowing past each second
options.explanation: One amp means one coulomb arriving every second.

options.text: in series with the component being measured
options.explanation: The meter must feel the same current as the component, so it sits in the same path.
That is the voltmeter's placement; an ammeter in parallel misreads the circuit.
Placement matters: only in series does it read the component's current.
Placing it across the cell measures the cell, not the component in question.

check.stem: Conventional current is taken to flow:

options.text: negative terminal back to the positive one
options.explanation: That is the direction of electron flow, not conventional current.

options.text: in the same direction as the electrons move
options.explanation: Electrons are negative, so they drift against the conventional arrow.

options.text: positive terminal out to the negative one
options.explanation: The convention sends current out of the positive terminal and back into the negative one.
Current travels the whole loop, wires included.

check.stem: A charge of 6 C flows past a point in a circuit in 2 s. The current is:

options.explanation: That multiplies charge by time instead of dividing.
That divides time by charge, flipping the ratio.
Current = charge ÷ time = 6 ÷ 2 = 3 A.
Adding the two quantities is meaningless here.

check.stem: State what electric current measures and give its unit.
check.modelAnswer: Current measures the rate at which electric charge flows through a component, and it is measured in amperes (A).

check.stem: How should an ammeter be connected when measuring the current through a lamp?
check.modelAnswer: In series with the lamp, so the same current that passes through the lamp also passes through the meter.

check.stem: Explain why scientists describe current as flowing from positive to negative even though electrons move the other way.
check.modelAnswer: The positive-to-negative direction was chosen as the convention before electrons were discovered, and scientists kept it after the electron turned out to drift the opposite way.

check.stem: A charge of 15 C flows through a torch bulb in 60 s. Calculate the current.
check.modelAnswer: Current = charge ÷ time = 15 C ÷ 60 s = 0.25 A.

lessons.title: Charge
lessons.opening: Inside the wires, the story gets specific: the movers are electrons, each carrying one negative packet of charge. This lesson names the carriers, then packages the whole picture into one equation — charge equals current multiplied by time — that turns meter readings into totals.
keyPoints: In solid metal conductors the current is a flow of negatively charged electrons.
Wires are made of metal because it conducts electricity well.
Charge, current and time are linked by Q = I × t.
Charge is measured in coulombs (C), current in amperes (A) and time in seconds (s).
Electron flow runs from negative to positive — the reverse of conventional current.

low.restatement: Multiply how hard the charge flows (current) by how long it flows (time) and you have the total charge delivered.
low.analogy: A water meter: flow rate times running time gives the total volume collected in the tank.
low.examPointer: Keep units straight — coulombs for charge, amperes for current, seconds for time — before substituting anything.

medium.restatement: The equation is a rate statement rearranged: since I = Q ÷ t, multiplying both sides by t gives Q = I × t.
medium.analogy: Earnings: current is your hourly wage, time is hours worked, and total charge is the pay packet at the end.
medium.examPointer: Convert minutes to seconds before substituting — examiners hide the unit conversion inside the question.

check.stem: In a metal wire, the charge carriers that make up the current are:

options.text: positive ions fixed in the metal lattice
options.explanation: Lattice ions vibrate in place; they do not drift along the wire.

options.text: free electrons, which carry negative charge
options.explanation: Metal conductors conduct through their negatively charged electrons.
Nuclear protons never roam a circuit wire.

options.text: whole atoms drifting along the wire
options.explanation: Atoms stay in the lattice; only their loose electrons travel.

check.stem: The equation linking charge, current and time is:

options.explanation: Dividing by time gives the current, not the charge.
Charge accumulates at the rate I for a duration t.
That inverts the rate relationship.
Different units cannot simply be added.

check.stem: How much charge flows when a current of 4 A runs for 10 s?

options.explanation: That divides time by current instead of multiplying.
Adding current and time is meaningless.
That divides current by time, giving the wrong direction.

check.stem: Electrons drift through a cell from:

options.text: positive to negative, like conventional current
options.explanation: Electrons are negative, so they move against the conventional arrow.

options.text: negative to positive, opposite to conventional current
options.explanation: Negative carriers drift the opposite way to the conventional direction.
The drift has one net direction around the loop.

options.text: nowhere — electrons stay fixed in the metal
options.explanation: Fixed electrons could never carry a current.

check.stem: A current quoted as 10 mA expressed in amperes is:

options.explanation: That scales the wrong way: milli means one thousandth.
That ignores the milli prefix entirely.
That treats milli as one tenth.

check.stem: Write down the equation linking charge, current and time, stating the unit of each quantity.
check.modelAnswer: Q = I × t, with charge Q in coulombs (C), current I in amperes (A) and time t in seconds (s).

check.stem: What carries the current inside a metal wire?
check.modelAnswer: A flow of negatively charged electrons drifts through the metal when a voltage drives them.

check.stem: Explain why conventional current and electron flow point in opposite directions.
check.modelAnswer: Conventional current was fixed as the direction positive charge would move, before anyone knew electrons existed; once electrons were found to be negative carriers, their drift turned out to run the other way, but the convention was kept.

check.stem: A motor draws a current of 0.5 A for 2 minutes. Calculate the charge that flows through it.
check.modelAnswer: Convert first: 2 minutes = 120 s. Then Q = I × t = 0.5 × 120 = 60 C.

glossary.definition: The rate at which electric charge streams through a component, measured in amperes.
The unit of current: one coulomb of charge passing each second.
The fundamental electrical quantity whose flow constitutes a current, measured in coulombs.
The unit of charge — the packet delivered by a one-amp current in one second.
The agreed direction of current, from the positive terminal to the negative one.
The negatively charged particle whose drift through a metal carries the current.

workedExample.prompt: A multiple-choice ask wants to know when an 8 A current will pass through a circuit. The options pair different charges with different times.
steps: Rearrange Q = I × t to make the current the subject: I = Q ÷ t.
Test the pairing 4 C in 0.5 s: I = 4 ÷ 0.5 = 8 A — this one matches.
Test 8 C in 0.1 s: I = 8 ÷ 0.1 = 80 A, far larger than 8 A.
Test 1 C in 8 s: I = 1 ÷ 8 = 0.125 A, far smaller than 8 A.
The remaining option (8 J used by 1 C) describes 8 volts, not 8 amperes.
workedExample.finalAnswer: A charge of 4 C passing in 0.5 s produces the 8 A current, so that option is the answer.
